cim_eredeti: Bolivian Engineer Built the First AI That Speaks Aymara — and Officials Are Already Using It
szoveg_eredeti:
More than 1.5 million Bolivians identify as Aymara, yet until now, no everyday voice-enabled AI assistant spoke back in their language.

That gap ends with Luzi — a voice-enabled artificial intelligence tool built entirely in El Alto, Bolivia, by a 30-year-old engineer who created it specifically so that indigenous speakers could access technology in their own tongue.

Ramos grew up watching a specific problem repeat itself across El Alto — Bolivia's second-largest city, home to nearly 886,000 residents perched above 4,000 meters. Farmers descending from the altiplano to sell potatoes, corn, and fruit couldn't negotiate with Spanish-speaking buyers. Crime victims who spoke only Aymara struggled to file police reports. Students in rural schools had no digital tools in their native language.

"I saw it was necessary to create an AI assistant so that people from rural areas would feel included and no longer disconnected — so they'd feel comfortable with technology and with communicating with people in El Alto," Ramos told EFE.

He built Luzi to address all three pressure points at once.

After mapping out the basic system with two fellow engineers, Ramos realized the biggest hurdle wasn't coding—it was the language itself. Because Aymara builds words and sentences in a completely different way than Spanish, he had to hire a linguist to map out how people actually speak and write it before the AI could sound natural.

That work paid off. Luzi now runs on a common digital platform designed for accessibility, with Ramos actively developing versions for Android and iOS so it can reach users on the phones already in their pockets.

The assistant's voice was not chosen at random. Ramos modeled it after the cholitas — the iconic Aymara women of La Paz — specifically to make Luzi feel familiar and close to the communities it serves, rather than like a corporate product imported from elsewhere.

Initial field tests ran into an unexpected wall: in some rural sectors, technology itself carries a cultural stigma. Ramos responded by holding hands-on training sessions that walked communities through the tool, and resistance gradually gave way to routine use.

The turning point came when El Alto's citizen security directorate adopted Luzi to assist Aymara speakers navigating the criminal justice system — people reporting crimes or seeking help who had previously been unable to communicate with Spanish-only officials. A school in Laja, La Paz, followed, integrating Luzi into classroom instruction for both students and teachers drafting documents in Aymara.

For that work, the Federación de Empresarios de El Alto recognized Ramos with a medal naming him revelación en tecnología 2026 — technology revelation of the year.

Ramos isn't stopping at Aymara. His roadmap calls for adding Quechua — spoken across Bolivia's western highlands and valleys — and Guaraní, the dominant indigenous language of the Chaco lowlands, turning Luzi into a multilingual platform capable of serving the country's three largest indigenous-speaking communities under one interface.

Separately, he is developing Vigía 360, a facial-recognition system built on AI-enabled security cameras aimed at identifying suspects and locating missing persons — a project that reflects his broader ambition to apply artificial intelligence to public safety challenges specific to Bolivia's urban centers.

The name Luzi itself carries that sense of local rootedness. Ramos derived it from Lucy — one of the most common given names in El Alto — then changed two letters to give the assistant what he called "its own identity." The result is a tool that is both technically novel and culturally grounded: an AI that didn't parachute in from Silicon Valley, but grew out of a specific city's specific needs.

cim: Luzi: megjelent az első ajmara nyelven beszélő AI-asszisztens
lead: Egy bolíviai mérnök kifejlesztette a Luzi nevű hangalapú AI-asszisztenst, amely az ajmara őslakos közösség mindennapi és hivatalos ügyintézését segíti.
osszefoglalo:
Juan David Ramos Cadena bolíviai mérnök megalkotta a **Luzi** nevű hangalapú AI-asszisztenst, amely az ajmara nyelvet beszélő 1,5 millió őslakos számára teszi hozzáférhetővé a digitális eszközöket. Mivel az ajmara nyelv szerkezete jelentősen eltér a spanyoltól, a fejlesztéshez nyelvészt is bevontak, így az eszköz természetes hanghordozással képes kommunikálni.

Az asszisztens hangját a helyi ajmara nőkről mintázták, hogy a felhasználók számára ismerős és elfogadható legyen. A rendszert El Alto város közbiztonsági igazgatóságán már élesben használják a spanyolul nem beszélő bűncselekmény-áldozatok segítésére, emellett iskolákban is alkalmazzák a tananyag és a dokumentumok elkészítéséhez.

A fejlesztő jelenleg az Android- és iOS-applikációkon dolgozik, a jövőben pedig a kecsua és a guarani nyelveket is integrálni tervezi a platformba.
miert_szamit: A projekt kiváló példa arra, hogy a speciális nyelvi adatkészletekre épülő **lokális AI-modell** olyan valós társadalmi és adminisztrációs problémákat tud megoldani, amelyeket a nagy globális rendszerek nem fednek le.
